Drive
drīv
v. (to force or urge along; to expel; rendering Hebrew garash, nadaph, Greek ekballo)
From Saxon drifan, to urge or impel. The word's first appearance in Scripture is the expulsion from Eden, and it keeps that weight: what is driven is not led but forced, whether chaff by wind or a man from a garden.

Biblical Definition

To drive is to move a thing by force rather than by consent. Its first use sets the pattern: “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). The driving out is judicial, and the guarded way says that man cannot simply walk back. From that beginning the word carries the sense of what has no root and no weight of its own: “The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away” (Psalm 1:4). The righteous man of the Psalm is a planted tree; the ungodly is chaff, and the judgment needs no violence beyond a wind, because there is nothing there to hold. The New Testament applies the same figure to the double-minded man in prayer: he “is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (James 1:6), which is why such a man is told not to expect to receive anything of the Lord. Scripture also puts the verb to a merciful use in the discipline of children: “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). Folly is bound in and must be driven out.

Webster 1828 Definition

To urge or press forward by force; to impel; to compel to move; to expel or chase away. Scripture uses it of the expulsion from Eden, of chaff before the wind, of the unstable soul, and of folly driven from a child by correction.

expand to see more

DRIVE, v.t. [Sax. drifan, to urge, impel.] To impel or urge forward by force; to force; to move by physical force; as, to drive cattle; to drive a nail.

2. To compel or urge by other means than absolute physical force; to constrain; as, hunger drives men to labor.

3. To chase; to hunt; to expel; as, to drive an enemy from his ground.

4. To guide and regulate the course of a carriage or the beasts that draw it.

5. To carry on; to prosecute; as, to drive a trade.

DRIVE, v.i. To be forced along; to be impelled; as, a ship drives before the wind. To rush with violence; to aim at or tend to.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:24 — "So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life."

Psalm 1:4 — "The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away."

James 1:6 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."

Proverbs 22:15 — "Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child; but the rod of correction shall drive it far from him."

Modern Corruption

The expulsion from Eden is read as a myth about growing up rather than as a judicial act, and the correction that drives folly from a child is renamed as harm — so both of Scripture's drivings are explained away.

expand to see more

Genesis 3:24 is regularly retold as the story of humanity leaving innocence behind, a necessary passage into maturity, with the cherubim and the flaming sword treated as symbols of an inward loss. That reading empties the sentence. The man is driven, by God, from a real garden, and the way to the tree of life is guarded so that he cannot return on his own terms — which is the whole reason a way back had to be opened by Another. Where the expulsion becomes a metaphor for maturation, the atonement becomes unnecessary, since nothing objective was ever barred.

The second corruption touches Proverbs 22:15. Correction administered by a father under God is now widely classed as harm as such, without distinction between the rod of correction and the cruelty Scripture equally condemns. The proverb states a diagnosis before it prescribes: foolishness is bound in the heart of a child, and something bound must be driven out rather than waited out. Fathers are to be gentle, never provoking their children to wrath (Ephesians 6:4), and they are to correct. Recover both halves and the word keeps its proper severity in judgment and its proper tenderness in the home. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the modern re-description of correction as 'harm' in order to rebut it

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew garash (to drive out, expel) is the verb of Eden and of the nations driven before Israel; nadaph (to drive asunder) gives Psalm 1 its chaff; Greek ekballo (to cast out) and elauno (to drive) carry the New Testament senses.

expand to see more

Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, cast out, expel; used of Adam from the garden and of the Canaanites from the land.

Hebrew nadaph (H5086) — to drive asunder, to scatter as chaff before wind; the verb of Psalm 1:4.

Hebrew muwcar (H4148) — chastening, correction, discipline; the instrument that drives folly out in Proverbs 22:15.

Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, drive out; used of casting out devils and of the Spirit driving our Lord into the wilderness.

Greek anemizo (G416) — to be driven by the wind; the picture of the wavering man in James 1:6.

Usage

"“So he drove out the man” — the expulsion is judicial, and the way back is guarded."

"“Like the chaff which the wind driveth away” — what has no root needs no violence to remove it."

"“The rod of correction shall drive it far from him” — bound folly is driven out, not outgrown."
